analysis.one_liner: Caps what drug makers can charge Americans at the lowest price charged in other developed countries.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced May 14, 2025 with three cosponsors, sits in the Senate health committee with no action taken since it was referred.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to set an annual reference price for every prescription drug, based on the lowest price charged in 12 peer countries like Canada, France, Japan, and the UK. Drug makers could not charge the government programs — Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA, federal employees, and Indian Health Service — more than that price. It also requires manufacturers to sell at the reference price to everyone else, insured or not, and fines violators five times the overcharge, with the penalties routed to NIH research.
analysis.who_benefits: People on Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, VA care, and other federal health programs, plus privately insured and uninsured Americans, who would pay no more for a drug than what it costs in the cheapest of 12 other developed countries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in federal health programs and beyond

how_it_helps.text: Caps drug prices for Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA, Federal Employees Health Benefits, and Indian Health Service at the lowest retail list price among 12 reference countries including Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the UK [S2].
Requires manufacturers to sell every drug at the reference price to all individuals, including the uninsured and people on private insurance, not just federal programs [S2].
Imposes a civil penalty of five times the overcharge for noncompliance, and sends the collected penalties to the National Institutes of Health for drug research and development [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose the ability to charge US programs and patients more than the lowest price available in other developed countries.

drawbacks.text: Tighter price limits could reduce manufacturers' revenue and investment in developing new medicines, the strongest good-faith objection to international reference pricing; the bill anticipates this partly by directing penalty revenue to NIH drug research [S2].

The cap applies to the retail list price, while much drug pricing is negotiated through rebates and discounts behind the list price, so the actual savings for patients could be smaller than the headline suggests unless list prices reflect real prices [S2].

For drugs not available in at least three reference countries, the price would be set by the Secretary's judgment on therapeutic value, R&D costs, and access — a large amount of discretion in one agency [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is large and direct: US drug prices are often several times higher than in peer countries, and the bill extends the cap beyond government programs to everyone. The main cost falls on pharmaceutical companies, whose lower revenue could somewhat slow new drug development. On balance, the design is simple and enforceable, with the biggest design question being whether list-price caps capture the rebates that currently lower real-world prices.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat without a markup or vote since May 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the End Price Gouging for Medications Act on May 14, 2025, joined by Sens. Welch, Sanders, and Durbin [S1].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which is the last recorded action [S4].
The bill has three cosponsors — two Senate Democrats and one independent [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers keep current prices for now; patients keep paying higher drug prices.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set the reference-price framework capping drug prices at the lowest peer-country price.

for.name: Sens. Peter Welch, Bernie Sanders, and Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction [S1]; Welch and Sanders are independents, Durbin a Democrat [S3].

for.name: 2 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only members to sign on beyond the sponsor [S3].

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no recorded action — no markup, no vote — since May 2025 [S4].

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has long campaigned against international reference-pricing proposals, which it warns would cut revenue and investment in new medicines; the bill's sponsor frames it directly against drug company pricing.

sides.party_line_note: All four original sponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-led pipeline in committee has produced no action.

industries.note: The bill would cap their US prices at the lowest peer-country price, including for privately insured and uninsured buyers, with fines of five times the overcharge — the industry's revenue from the American market, the world's highest-priced, is the direct target. Its interest in keeping US prices high runs against patients' interest in paying less.
Insurers bear part of drug costs today; a hard price cap would lower what they pay for the drugs they cover, and the bill counts employer-plan coverage plus cost-sharing toward the cap.
Federal and state health programs would pay less for covered drugs, reducing government and premium-payer spending.
Penalties collected from noncompliant manufacturers are transferred annually to NIH for drug research and development funding.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, three cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action since referral in May 2025, the bill is very unlikely to advance; a companion bill in the House and GOP buy-in to reference pricing would be needed for any movement, and most one-sponsor drug pricing bills die in committee.
